To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) submarine melting of Greenland’s outlet glaciers is driven by multiple overturning cells that are organized by stratification in the waters that reach the glacier margins and (2) these overturning cells are present in both summer and winter and hence the melt dynamics are not driven solely by the glacier’s discharge.
submarine melt rates at Greenland’s glaciers are controlled by multiple overturning cells in the stratified waters that reach the ice margin.

(i) the submarine melt rate of Greenland’s glaciers is controlled by both Arctic and Atlantic waters, and (ii) the circulation at the glacier terminus is organized in multiple overturning cells that are driven by the different properties of the two water masses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between ocean and glacier and the impact of ocean stratification.
the dynamics and evolution of the Greenland Ice sheet and its response to climate change.
the impact of ocean stratification at the ice-ocean boundary on the melting of a major outlet glacier in Greenland.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stratification of the fjord waters is a key control of the submarine melt rate of Greenland outlet glaciers, and hence of the stability of the Greenland Ice sheet.
the submarine melt rate is controlled by the interaction of multiple overturning cells, each driven by the different properties of the water masses that are present in the fjords.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stratification is a key factor that determines the submarine melt rates of Greenland glaciers.
the melt rate is not controlled by the overturning of the fjord water, but by the vertical heat flux across the interface.

submarine melt rates at the terminus of Greenland’s tidewater glaciers depend on the circulation of Atlantic and Arctic waters at the ice/oceans interface, which is controlled by the fjords’ stratification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
submarine melting is not controlled by a single process, but is instead the outcome of complex interactions between the ocean and the ice sheet.
the submarine melt rate is not a function of a single overturning circulation, but is rather a complex function of the stratification and circulation at the ice front.
the submarine melt rate is not only a function of the water column density, as is often assumed, but also of its stability.
